summaries.example: Imagine these steps: If every blue card is shiny, and this card is blue, then this card is shiny. The result does not depend on what the card is made of. The same pattern works for cats, books, or planets. Logicians call this kind of repeatable reasoning a logical pattern.
summaries.summary: A logical truth is a statement whose truth seems to come from reasoning itself rather than from special facts about the world. For example, if all cats are mysterious and Drasha is a cat, then Drasha is mysterious. The names and subject matter can change, but the reasoning pattern remains. This is called formality. Philosophers also say logical truths have a special modal force: they must be true, or could not be false, in some sense. They disagree about what this means. Some connect necessity with all possible situations; others explain it through general rules about actual things, accepted cases, or ways of making inferences. Some also connect logical truth with a priori knowledge, meaning knowledge that does not depend on observation. Modern logic studies these questions by building formal languages with exact symbols, grammars, and proof rules. It also studies validity in mathematical structures, where a formula is valid if it is true in every suitable structure. These methods are powerful, but the entry explains why it remains difficult to show that any mathematical method perfectly matches the philosophical idea of logical truth.
key_ideas: Logical truths are supposed to have a special kind of necessity: they must be true, or cannot be false, in some important sense.
Many philosophers think logical truths are formal. Their truth depends on a pattern, not on the special subject matter.
People disagree about what necessity means. It might involve every possible situation, every suitable replacement of words, or the way we reason.
Formal logic uses exact symbols, rules, and mathematical structures to study logical truth, but philosophers still ask whether these tools capture the whole idea.
summaries.why_it_matters: Logical reasoning appears in mathematics, science, computer programs, and everyday thinking. Understanding logical truth helps us see why some arguments work even when their topics change. It also teaches an important lesson about philosophy: a useful formal method may not settle every question about what logic really is.

important_terms.definition: A statement that follows from its logical pattern and is treated as unable to be false in the relevant sense.
The idea that something must be true, or could not be false, in some sense.
A general pattern that stays the same when particular words are replaced by other words.
A careful language made with clear symbols and rules so that reasoning can be studied exactly.

questions_to_think_about: Is a rule still true when we replace its topic with a completely different topic?
Does “must be true” mean true in every possible situation, or only true whenever the pattern is used correctly?
Can a computer-like list of rules capture every logical truth?
Why might a sentence about a real object be true without being a logical truth?

summaries.example: Consider the argument: If no Q is R, and some P is Q, then some P is not R. Let Q mean “musician,” R mean “silent person,” and P mean “student.” If no musician is silent and at least one student is a musician, then at least one student is not silent. The argument depends on its quantifier and conditional structure, not on the meanings of “musician” or “student.” That is why it illustrates formality. But the broader philosophical question remains: does every substitution preserving this form count as a logical truth, and does formal validity fully capture logical necessity?
summaries.summary: The entry examines what logical truth is and whether mathematical logic captures it. Standard examples have an inference pattern such as: if all P are Q and a is P, then a is Q. Their apparent necessity does not seem to depend on the subject matter. This motivates two broad ideas. First, logical truths have modal force: they are said to be necessary, impossible to falsify, or true across some range of possible circumstances or cases. Philosophers disagree about whether this force reduces to generalizations over actual items, concerns counterfactual worlds, reflects accepted cases, or belongs to the use of logic in reasoning. A related dispute concerns a priori status and analyticity: some philosophers explain logical knowledge through rational insight, convention, or conceptual analysis, while others treat logic as deeply embedded in practice or reject strictly a priori knowledge. Second, logical truth is often said to be formal. A logical form is a schema in which logical expressions such as conditionals, conjunctions, and quantifiers remain fixed while non-logical expressions vary. If formality is correct, appropriate replacement instances of a logical form should preserve logical truth. Yet no agreed test identifies all and only logical expressions. The entry then turns to formalization, derivability, and model-theoretic validity. Formal systems make symbols, grammar, axioms, and inference rules exact. A formula is derivable when it results from axioms by specified rules; it is model-theoretically valid when it is true in every mathematical structure of the appropriate kind. For first-order languages, completeness links these notions. For higher-order languages, incompleteness and questions about the status of higher-order quantifiers prevent an equally simple result
key_ideas: The entry distinguishes two central ideas about logical truth: modal force and formality. Neither has a universally accepted interpretation.
Modal force may be understood as truth in all counterfactual circumstances, truth under general substitutions, truth in all relevant cases, or a feature of reasoning and knowledge.
Formality requires that the truth survive suitable replacements of non-logical expressions. This helps explain why a merely necessary or analytic statement need not be a logical truth.
The classification of logical expressions is itself disputed. Proposals include wide applicability, invariance under permutations, and meaning supplied by purely inferential rules.
Formalization makes grammar, meanings, and deductions precise. It supports mathematical characterizations through derivability and model-theoretic validity.

For standard first-order languages, Gödel’s completeness theorem links derivability and model-theoretic validity, supporting their extensional adequacy under many ordinary conceptions. Higher-order languages create deeper problems because their calculi are incomplete with respect to standard model-theoretic validity.
summaries.why_it_matters: Logic provides tools for checking arguments in mathematics, science, philosophy, and computing. But the philosophical study of logical truth asks a deeper question than whether a proof is correct: what makes a logical truth logical? The distinction between modality, formality, derivability, and validity shows why a mathematically precise system can be extremely useful without automatically resolving every conceptual dispute. It also clarifies why disagreements about logical constants and higher-order reasoning affect the foundations of mathematics.

important_terms.definition: A truth understood as necessary in a logical sense, though philosophers disagree about the exact kind of necessity involved.
A claim about what could not be false or what must be true; in this debate, it may concern possible circumstances, generality, or knowledge.
A sentence’s abstract schema, obtained by distinguishing logically important expressions from replaceable non-logical material.
The feature that a logical truth’s appropriate replacement instances are also logical truths.
Knowledge or justification that does not depend on empirical observation or experiment.
A precise symbolic language with specified vocabulary, formation rules, and meanings designed for exact logical study.
A formula’s being true in every structure allowed for its language, as defined using mathematical semantics.
Being obtainable from stated axioms by a finite sequence of explicitly specified inference rules.

questions_to_think_about: If a statement is true in every possible circumstance, is that enough to make it a logical truth?
Should logical expressions be identified by their meaning, their inferential use, their wide applicability, or some structural property?
Does model-theoretic validity analyze logical truth, merely model it, or provide a mathematically useful substitute?
Why does incompleteness for higher-order calculi make it difficult to assess derivability and validity?
Could more than one collection of cases legitimately determine what counts as logically true?

summaries.example: Suppose a coach says: “If every member of Team A finished the puzzle, and Maya is on Team A, then Maya finished the puzzle.” Now replace “Team A” with “the library books,” “Maya” with “this book,” and “finished the puzzle” with “has a label.” The subject changes, but the reasoning pattern stays. A logician may call the pattern logical because it works through many replacements. Still, philosophers can ask whether all such replacements count, and whether the pattern is true because of a deep necessity or simply because it is a reliable rule.
summaries.summary: The SEP entry asks what separates logical truths from other truths. A logical truth is usually thought to have a special force: it must be true, or could not be false, in an important sense. But philosophers disagree about the meaning of this necessity. Some understand it through a pattern that remains true for every appropriate replacement of its topic-specific terms. Others connect it with truth in possible situations, truth in all relevant cases, or the way different kinds of reasoning operate. A related issue is whether logical truths are a priori, meaning knowable without observation, and whether they are analytic, meaning true through meanings or concepts. Another major idea is formality. The logical form of a sentence is its abstract pattern. In “If all cats are mysterious and Drasha is a cat, then Drasha is mysterious,” the names and descriptive words can be replaced while the logical words and arrangement remain. On this view, a logical truth should have logical-truth replacements. Yet it is difficult to define logical expressions exactly. Suggestions include that they apply across many subjects, remain unchanged when individuals are permuted, or get their meaning from purely inferential rules. Modern logic studies these questions using formalization: exact symbols, grammar, axioms, and inference rules. It also defines validity using mathematical structures. Derivability concerns what can be produced by a calculus; model-theoretic validity concerns what is true in every permitted structure. In standard first-order logic, a completeness theorem connects them. Higher-order logic is more controversial because no sound calculus captures all of its usual model-theoretic validities, and philosophers disagree about what this tells us about logical truth.
key_ideas: Logical truths are often contrasted with ordinary facts. “Drasha is a cat, and all cats are mysterious, so Drasha is mysterious” seems to work because of its structure.
Philosophers disagree about the meaning of “must.” It could refer to all possible situations, all relevant cases, general rules about actual things, or accepted ways of reasoning.
Formality says that the truth of a logical pattern should not depend on special names or topics. However, it is hard to agree on exactly which words are logical.
Some philosophers connect logic with a priori knowledge or analyticity; others argue that logic is learned from experience, built into our thinking, or justified in a different way.
Formal systems use symbols, grammar, axioms, and rules. A formula can be derivable by rules or valid in every mathematical structure.

For ordinary first-order systems, derivability and model-theoretic validity fit together especially well. Higher-order systems raise harder questions, including whether their quantifiers are genuinely logical.
summaries.why_it_matters: These ideas help explain why the same reasoning can work in geometry, biology, or everyday planning. They also show why formal logic is both powerful and limited: it can make rules exact, while leaving open philosophical questions about necessity, meaning, and which symbols belong to logic. Studying those questions helps students understand the foundations of mathematics and careful argument.

important_terms.definition: A statement that is true because of its logical structure and is often thought to have a special kind of necessity.
The philosophical idea of what must be true or what could have been different.
The underlying reasoning pattern of a sentence, separating general logical words from topic-specific words.
The principle that changing topic-specific parts of a logical pattern should preserve logical truth in suitable cases.
Knowledge that is supposed to be available without relying on observation or experiment.
A symbolic system with exact rules for building sentences and carrying out deductions.
A formula’s being true in every mathematical interpretation or structure allowed by a formal language.

questions_to_think_about: Why does changing the topic of an argument sometimes leave its reasoning unchanged?
Can a statement be necessary without being a logical truth?
What makes words such as “all,” “some,” “if,” and “and” different from words such as “cat” or “mysterious”?
Would a perfect list of proof rules settle what all logical truths are?
Why might philosophers disagree about whether logical truths are known without experience?
